title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s refrigeration sabotage as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks
items.content_text: France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against the people behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers, freezing their assets and barring travel, a day after EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed new Iran sanctions are being prepared. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned on 16 November that settings were also changed at French blood-service sites, putting donor blood and therapies at risk. US and Israeli officials have told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers also sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. For OT defenders the lesson is plain: any internet-reachable controller is now a proven target.

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. On 10 November Sweden warned that more incidents are likely after refrigeration was tampered with at seven Coop stores and an undisclosed number of ICA stores on 2 November; its NCSC says the victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer protected by weak passwords. On 12 November Belgium’s interior minister said evidence on the Belgian attacks points to Iran but stopped short of an official attribution (see top story); a pro-Russian claim is unverified, and France has formally attributed only the separate 12 October attack, to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Exposure is falling but not gone: exposed Danfoss StoreView instances dropped from 3,004 to 708 between 9 October and 5 November (The Hacker News, 9 November). Sekoia reported on 10 November that the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account, apparently a step towards resetting its password, and assesses that both waves may come from the same actor. If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today.

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, about a week after fixes shipped, then used a local flaw in the gateway’s DynamicCLI service (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted web shells and backdoors named TSGA and TSProxy, scanned the internal network, moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper that overwrites and deletes files. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached gateways in several countries and sectors with no destruction seen. The backdoors resemble tooling linked to the China-nexus group UNC5221, but Check Point does not attribute the campaign with confidence. CISA added CVE-2026-123039 to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi hosts often run HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified on 29 October that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to gain root on about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October, then stole Active Directory credentials. Victims were in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. The OT exposure keeps widening: Siemens lists Spectrum Power grid-control systems and AMIS TS, and on 16 November added its WTV676 and WTV776 metering gateways (all versions, no fix), Schneider lists a Foxboro DCS server, and ABB lists Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways, several with no fix yet. Attribution is suspected, not confirmed, and no Siemens, Schneider or ABB product is reported exploited. No OT operator has been named, so treat this as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: A Chilean solar-and-battery plant is still off the grid nearly three months after a cyberattack, and lawmakers want answers
items.content_text: The 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant in Chile’s Tarapacá region, with a 98 MW / 312 MWh battery system still in commissioning, has been disconnected from the national grid since late August after a cyberattack. Chile’s National Electric Coordinator triggered its disconnection protocol on 27 August after the owner reported the attack, and its 14 November daily report still lists both assets at zero availability under forced outage. The coordinator calls the case exceptional and is withholding details while it investigates. On 11 November a member of Congress asked the security and energy ministries whether the national cybersecurity agency was notified as Chilean law requires and which control systems were hit; no answer had been published by 16 November. The owner, entry route and affected systems are undisclosed. Two suspected attacks on plants in Coquimbo the next day were reportedly ruled out. For renewables operators, the lesson is how long a plant stays dark once it is pulled off the grid for safety and cannot be restored with confidence (editorial assessment).

items.title: Equinor says the cyberattack on its IT systems has been stopped after three days, as a second Norwegian energy firm reports an attempted attack
items.content_text: Equinor, Norway’s state-controlled energy company and the largest supplier of pipeline gas to the EU, said on the morning of 20 November that the cyberattack on certain IT systems it first disclosed on 17 November has been stopped. Production ran normally throughout, and the company says it has found no sign that data was stolen or altered, or any effect on employees, partners or suppliers. During the incident Equinor said the attack was not a self-spreading virus, that it had a clear view of how it was carried out and which systems were hit, and on 19 November that it did not appear aimed specifically at the company. It has reported the matter to police and worked with Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM), which raised the national cyber risk level to “high” on 27 October. A day after Equinor’s first report, power utility Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack; it says operations were unaffected and it has seen no misuse of data. Neither company has disclosed the entry route or the attacker, and nothing reported points to OT. Two incidents at Norwegian energy firms in one week are still a reason for energy operators to check their IT-to-OT boundaries now (editorial assessment).

items.title: Illinois investigates an apparent cyberattack attempt on the Algonquin Dam on the Fox River
items.content_text: The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said on 20 November that its Office of Water Resources detected an apparent attempted cyberattack on the Algonquin Dam, about 45 miles northwest of Chicago, on Monday 16 November. Staff acted at once to block the unauthorised access, and the department says the dam stayed secure and fully operational. It has not said which system was targeted, how the attempt was spotted or whether gate controls were reachable. Illinois State Police, the state emergency-management and technology agencies and CISA are investigating, and IDNR says it is working with state and federal partners to secure dams across Illinois. The department said it had no sign of a link to other recent attacks or outages, and no group has been named. For dam and flood-control owners it is a timely prompt to check who and what can reach gate and spillway controls remotely (editorial assessment).

items.title: Ransomware halts smart-meter production and shipments at Japan’s Osaki Electric
items.content_text: Osaki Electric, a Japanese maker of electricity smart meters, said ransomware encrypted data on its servers on 17 November. It confirmed the attack at about 10:35 a.m. local time, cut its systems off from outside networks around midday, and suspended production and shipments of smart meters and other products at its Saitama R&D and manufacturing centre and at group production companies Iwate Osaki Electric and Osaki Platech. NHK reported on 18 November that the production-management system was among the systems knocked out. Outside specialists are checking whether data was stolen, and the company has informed police and customers. In a 20 November update the company said the intruder most likely got in at about 1:30 a.m. on 15 November through a VPN device, by repeated password guessing against an account without multi-factor authentication; some virtual servers were encrypted and technical information believed to come from its systems has been posted online. No group has claimed the attack. Nothing reported suggests meters already in the field or electricity supply are affected. For utilities, the risk is supply-chain: delayed meter rollouts, and the question of how a supplier protects the systems that build, configure and sign the devices it ships (editorial assessment).

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority forces manual workarounds at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The authority that runs the Port of Santos, Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on 6 November after a power fluctuation hit its servers, and on 10 November confirmed the outage was a cyberattack. Access-control and identification systems and digital tools used to coordinate port operations went down, so vessel, truck and train procedures were delayed and some automated checks, such as matching ship dimensions to berths, were done by hand. On 8 November São Paulo’s port security commission raised the port’s protection level to 2 of 3, adding police presence. Internet and phones were back on 9 November, and on 16 November the authority said its main internal systems were in final tests, with some services still running by email and about 70% of affected file backups recovered. Ship movements and landside access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the authority has not said who was behind it, how they got in or whether data was taken. For port and terminal operators, the lesson is that access control and berth planning are operational systems that need a tested manual fallback (editorial assessment).

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, with long-running espionage access later passed to teams pursuing destructive goals, sometimes disguised as ransomware or hacktivism, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For OT owners, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers.

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October.

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hackers probe 14 newly disclosed flaws in end-of-life Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers, five of which will never be fixed
items.content_text: VulnCheck has disclosed 14 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO, the Dixell supervisory system that runs supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, each of which gave its researcher root on test units. Nine affect only firmware built before a 2021 rewrite and include unauthenticated command execution and a hard-coded admin password. The other five reach the latest firmware: the daily admin password is derived from the device’s MAC address and the date, and the MAC address is visible without logging in, so an attacker can compute the password, turn on SSH and log in as root. VulnCheck’s sensors saw exploitation attempts against two older-firmware flaws within two hours of the 12 November CVE publication; it calls the sources opportunistic scanners, not the state campaign in France. Copeland ended XWEB EVO support on 16 March 2026 and will not fix the five current-firmware flaws; nearly 2,000 units are reachable from the internet. CyberScoop adds that XBOW honeypots posing as these controllers drew hundreds of requests and login attempts within a day, and someone changed the temperature on one simulated freezer.

items.title: Six unpatched pre-login flaws in Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers prompt Belgian, German and Irish warnings to pull them off the internet
items.content_text: Amsterdam consultancy Midnight Blue has disclosed six stack buffer overflows in Danfoss AK-SM 800A system managers, the store-level controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, that allow remote code execution without logging in; one works even with “strict” session control turned on. All firmware up to 5.3.2 is affected and CVEs are still pending. The BSI says the 5.4.0 package released this month is not affected, but Midnight Blue says 5.4.0 predates its research and does not fix these bugs, so treat 5.4.0 as unconfirmed until Danfoss says otherwise. The researchers say an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset or firmware update, or brick units, because the device does not appear to use secure boot; that is a stated possibility, not a demonstrated one. Belgium’s CCB and Germany’s BSI (13 November) and Ireland’s NCSC have all told operators that firmware updates, password changes and strict mode are not enough for internet-exposed units. Danfoss had published no advisory or fix date as of 16 November. No exploitation of these six flaws is reported.

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November, which it calls a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, missing authorization checks, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and it removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Remote control and Intune integration stay blocked for now. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud, forcing it to take the management portal and APIs offline; it says mail flow continued, it has found no access to customer data, and the breach is unrelated to N-central. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: SonicWall says its Gen 6 firewalls will get no more security patches and tells customers to pull them off the internet edge
items.content_text: SonicWall has told customers still running Generation 6 firewalls, which run SonicOS 6.x, to retire and replace them now and stop exposing them at the internet edge, because they will no longer receive security patches, even for critical flaws. The list covers TZ, SOHO, NSA, NSa, SuperMassive and NSsp models as well as the NSv virtual appliances. SonicWall says attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever, and it expects internet-facing Gen 6 units to be actively targeted. No new flaw or exploitation was announced with the warning. Small utilities, water systems and plants often rely on one of these boxes as the only barrier between remote access and the control network, so an unpatchable perimeter firewall is an OT exposure in its own right (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA flags trailer-brake controller takeover flaws, an OpenPLC admin-account race and an unfixed MQTT library bug, after Tuesday’s water SCADA advisory
items.content_text: CISA published three more ICS advisories on 19 November. The most serious covers Elecbrakes EB2, VM1 and ELBC2000 electronic trailer-brake controllers, used in Australia and New Zealand: an unprotected firmware-update channel, replayable authentication and a missing authentication check (CVSS v3.1 9.6) could let an attacker on an adjacent network take control of a trailer’s brakes, change its firmware, or disable brake lights and other safety features. Elecbrakes has released fixed firmware (EB2 3.0.4.4.3, installed through its app), while CISA lists ELBC2000 as affected in all versions. OpenPLC Runtime 4.2.4 and earlier has a race condition that lets concurrent requests create several unauthenticated admin accounts (fixed in 4.3.0), and the libumqtt MQTT client library has an integer underflow (CVSS v3.1 8.6) with no fix, because its maintainers did not respond to CISA. Tuesday’s batch led with six flaws in Dorsett Controls InfoScan water-utility SCADA, fixed in version 1.46, plus Siemens republications. CISA reports no known public exploitation of any of them.

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds water, food, rail, maritime and building-automation coverage
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management now led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions, and applying zero-trust principles. Many regulators, insurers and auditors use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what operators are asked to show; the comment window is the chance for practitioners to flag guidance that would not work on a plant floor.

items.title: GAO says USDA and FDA have left gaps in food-sector cyber threat sharing and emergency preparedness
items.content_text: The US Government Accountability Office reported on 19 November that the Agriculture Department and the Food and Drug Administration have met most of the food-sector cybersecurity requirements set by the 2021 defence authorization act, but only partly met or missed five of them. Staffing and resource limits have left gaps in how the agencies share threat and vulnerability information with the sector and in emergency preparedness. GAO warns that basic failures such as unchanged default passwords could let attackers manipulate food-quality, contamination-testing or traceability data, and that internet-connected farm equipment such as GPS-guided tractors could be compromised at scale. It cites the 2021 ransomware attack that shut down some of the world’s largest meat plants. With refrigeration controllers already under attack in Europe (see Incidents & Attacks), food and cold-chain operators should not wait for federal programmes to catch up (editorial assessment).

items.title: EU sanctions the pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16), which has hit energy, transport and water websites
items.content_text: On 16 November the EU Council added the pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16) to its cyber-sanctions list, alongside 30 people and a propaganda firm listed under its Russia hybrid-threat and cyber regimes. Listings bring asset freezes and a ban on making funds available to those named. The EU says the group has attacked government bodies, critical infrastructure and companies in Ukraine, the US and EU member states, mainly with denial-of-service attacks on websites in sectors including energy, transport and water supply. The same group posted an unverified claim for the November European refrigeration attacks (see Incidents & Attacks). Sanctions will not stop denial-of-service traffic, but they mark a shift from naming hacktivist fronts to penalising them; for OT teams the practical point is that these groups pick targets from whatever is reachable (editorial assessment).
